Expectation1: Help out during difficult times or emergencies.
Situation1: You get a frantic call from your friend whose car has broken down on the side of the highway late at night, and they need you to come get them immediately.
Situation2: They scan items during a slow afternoon with a few customers in line.
Story: I was standing behind the register, scanning groceries for the last few customers of the evening. The store was quiet, the hum of the fluorescent lights and the soft beep of the scanner filling the air. My phone buzzed in my pocket, and when I glanced at the screen, I saw it was my best friend, Sarah. I hesitated, but answered quickly, keeping my voice low. Her voice was shaky—her car had broken down on the highway, and she was scared, stranded in the dark. She begged me to come get her right away. My heart pounded. As a friend, I knew she needed me, and I could hear the panic in her voice. But as a cashier, I was still on shift, with customers waiting and my manager nearby. I could feel their eyes on me, expecting me to keep the line moving, to finish my work. I felt torn, caught between the urgent need to help my friend and the responsibility to my job. My hands trembled as I tried to focus on the groceries, my mind racing with what I should do next.
